blocks.text: What to look for when deciding for yourself. Establish first whether you are actually facing this decision, or simply investing a salary as it arrives, in which case there is no choice to make. If you do hold a sum, decide the schedule and its end date before the first purchase. Ask honestly what you would do if the market fell 25% in month two, since the strategy is worthless if you would stop. And treat the expected cost of averaging in as the price of a behavioural guarantee, which is a fair thing to buy.

Write down the sum you would invest, the number of months you would spread it over, and the date of the final purchase. Then write one sentence describing what you will do if prices fall sharply during the schedule. If that sentence says you would pause, rewrite the plan as a lump sum, because a schedule you would abandon at the low point delivers the cost of averaging in without the benefit.
One cost of averaging in is easy to overlook and straightforward to control.

Twelve purchases instead of one means twelve spreads, and where a platform charges per trade, twelve commissions. On a large sum this is trivial and on a small one it is not. Someone spreading 3,000 over twelve monthly purchases of 250 with a fixed charge per trade can lose a meaningful percentage to costs that a single purchase would have avoided.

Check the per-trade charge before choosing the number of instalments. Four quarterly purchases capture most of the behavioural benefit of twelve monthly ones at a third of the trading cost, and the difference between four and twelve instalments has very little effect on the outcome the research measures.

quiz.question: Vanguard found lump-sum investing beat dollar-cost averaging about two thirds of the time. What follows?
options: Dollar-cost averaging is a mistake and should never be used
Lump sum has the higher expected return, while averaging in reduces the chance of a regret-driven exit — a legitimate trade at a known cost
Lump sum always wins, so the timing decision does not matter
The research is unreliable because markets change
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Markets rise more often than they fall, so money waiting to be invested misses more rises than falls — that is where the two-thirds comes from. But in the other third averaging in does better, and its real value is behavioural: reducing the chance of an abandonment that costs far more than the expected difference.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Two thirds is not always, and the remaining third is exactly when averaging in helps. The finding says lump sum has the higher expected return; it does not say averaging in is a mistake, because reducing the chance of panic-selling has real value that the average return figure does not capture.

quiz.question: An investor spreads 12,000 over twelve months while the price falls from 100 to 75 and recovers to 105, ending with about 14,139. The same money invested at once would have been worth 12,600. What does this example prove?
options: That averaging in is the better strategy
Nothing beyond the mechanism — averaging in wins when prices fall during the schedule, and prices rise more often than they fall
That the investor timed the market successfully
That lump-sum investing is unsuitable for volatile markets
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Run the identical schedule against a market rising from 100 to 122 and averaging in finishes at about 13,241 against 14,640 for the lump sum. Neither outcome was knowable in advance, and since markets rise more often than they fall, the average case favours investing at once.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. A single favourable path is not evidence about the strategy. The same schedule loses in a rising market, and rising is the more common outcome — which is exactly why the research finds lump sum ahead about two thirds of the time.

quiz.question: Someone plans to average a sum in over twelve months but admits they would pause the schedule if the market fell 25% in month two. What should they do?
options: Proceed, since pausing during a fall is prudent
Recognise that a schedule they would abandon at the low point gives them the cost of averaging in without the benefit, and reconsider the plan
Extend the schedule to twenty-four months
Switch entirely to cash until the market is calm
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The benefit of averaging in comes precisely from continuing to buy while prices are low. Stopping at the low point removes the benefit and keeps the cost — the money that missed the rises. The plan needs to be one they would actually follow, or it is not a plan.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Pausing feels prudent and is the opposite of how the strategy works: the cheap purchases are the entire mechanism. A longer schedule makes the problem larger, and moving to cash abandons the decision rather than making it.

keyTerms.term: Kupunguza wastani wa bei kwa dola (DCA)
keyTerms.def: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals.
Investing the whole amount at once. Higher expected return, higher regret risk.

lessons.chapterTitle: Hatari na Upimaji wa Ukubwa wa Nafasi kwa Hisa
lessons.title: Margin, Leverage and Short Selling
lessons.keyIdea: Borrowing removes limited liability, and shorting removes the floor. Both convert a bad outcome into one that can exceed what you put in.

blocks.text: Everything so far assumed you invest money you have. Two common practices break that assumption, and both undo protections earlier lessons relied on.
Borrowing from a broker to buy more shares than your cash allows, using the shares themselves as collateral.
Margin multiplies the outcome in both directions, and the multiplication is straightforward.

You have 10,000 and borrow another 10,000, buying 20,000 of shares. A 20% rise makes 4,000 on your 10,000 — a 40% return before interest. A 20% fall loses 4,000, which is 40% of your money. The shares moved 20%; you moved 40%.

Lesson 1 said limited liability caps your loss at what you paid. Borrowing removes that cap. The loan is owed regardless of what the shares do, so a large enough fall can leave you owing money after the position is gone. An investment that cannot cost more than you put in is a different thing from one that can, and margin converts the first into the second.
There is also a mechanism that can force the loss to be realised at the worst possible moment.
A demand from the broker for more money when the collateral value falls too far. If it is not met, the broker sells your holdings to repay the loan.

This is what turns a temporary fall into a permanent loss. Chapter 3 Lesson 1 distinguished volatility, which you can wait out, from permanent loss, which you cannot. A margin call removes the ability to wait — the position is closed at the bottom, by someone else, and any later recovery happens without you.
Forex Chapter 3 Lesson 2 covered the same mechanism in that market. The instrument differs; the sequence does not.
Short selling inverts the position entirely.
Borrowing shares, selling them, and hoping to buy them back cheaper before returning them. A bet that the price falls.

The asymmetry from Lesson 1 now runs against you, and it is worth stating precisely. A share you own can fall to zero — you lose what you paid, and no more. A share you have shorted can rise without limit, and every unit of rise is your loss.

You short 100 shares at 50, receiving 5,000. If the price goes to zero you keep the 5,000 — that is the maximum possible gain. If it rises to 250 you must buy back at 25,000, losing 20,000 on a position that received 5,000. There is no level at which the loss stops.

A short can also be closed against your will. The lender can recall the borrowed shares at any time, forcing you to buy back immediately whatever the price. If many shorts are forced to buy at once, their buying drives the price up, forcing more of them to buy — a short squeeze. Chapter 5 examines the most famous recent example, and finds the popular explanation of it does not survive contact with the regulator's own report.

Shorting also carries an ongoing cost. You pay to borrow the shares, and on a heavily shorted company that fee can be substantial — so the position loses money while nothing happens, and being right eventually is not the same as being right in time.

Neither tool is illegitimate. Both are used competently by professionals every day. The point is that both remove a protection the rest of this track has been relying on, and neither belongs in a beginner's portfolio.
It is worth knowing how far a price has to move before a margin call arrives, because the answer is much closer than most borrowers assume.
The minimum proportion of a margined position that must be covered by your own money. Fall below it and the broker demands more or sells.

You put in 10,000, borrow 10,000, and hold 20,000 of shares. The maintenance requirement is 25%. Your equity is the value of the shares less the 10,000 loan, so the call arrives when the position is worth about 13,333 — a fall of just 33% in the shares. At that point your own money is down to about 3,333, a loss of two thirds, and the broker can sell without waiting for you.

A 33% fall is common. It is smaller than the fall in either case study in Chapter 5, and smaller than several ordinary corrections. Leverage does not create a distant catastrophic scenario; it converts an unremarkable market event into a forced sale at the worst available price.
The equivalent constraint on a short position is the cost of holding it, and that cost is not fixed.
The annual rate charged for borrowing shares to short. It rises with demand and can become extreme on a company many people want to short.

A short of 5,000 with a borrow fee of 20% a year costs 500 to hold for six months, before any price movement. If the shares are unchanged after six months, the position has lost 10% of its value doing nothing at all. On a heavily shorted company the rate can be far higher.

blocks.alt: A falling line showing the investors own money in a position of 10,000 borrowed against 10,000, as the share price falls. A marked threshold shows the margin call arriving at a fall of about 33 percent, when the position is worth 13,333 and the investors own money is down to 3,333.
blocks.caption: A 33 percent fall is unremarkable. Leverage converts it into a forced sale at the worst available price.

blocks.text: What to look for before using either. Establish the maintenance requirement and calculate the exact price at which a call arrives, in advance and in writing. Establish the interest rate on the loan, which is charged whether the position works or not. For a short, establish the borrow fee and whether the shares are hard to borrow, which is a warning that a recall is more likely. And ask whether you would survive the position being closed for you at the worst moment, because that is the scenario both instruments are built to produce.

Take any position you hold and calculate what it would look like with a loan of equal size. Write down the price at which a margin call would arrive at a 25% maintenance requirement, and how often the share has fallen that far in the last ten years. Most readers doing this find the answer is more than once, which is the most useful thing this lesson can tell you.
A third instrument packages leverage in a form that requires no borrowing and no margin account, which is what makes it dangerous.
A fund that aims to deliver a multiple of an index's return over a single day, resetting its exposure at the end of each day.

The words over a single day carry the whole risk. Because the exposure resets daily, the fund's return over any longer period depends on the path the index took, not only on where it ended. In a volatile market that moves up and down without going anywhere, the resetting mechanism loses money.

An index rises 10%, falls 9.09%, and repeats this three times, finishing exactly where it started. A twice-leveraged daily fund tracking it correctly every single day finishes down about 5.4%. Nothing malfunctioned and no fee caused it. The daily reset produced the loss, and a longer or more volatile period produces a larger one.

These funds are built for holding periods measured in days and are widely held for months. If you own one, check what its index has done over your holding period and compare it with what the fund has done. The gap is not a scandal — it is disclosed in the documentation — but almost nobody reads it before buying.

quiz.question: What is the maximum possible loss on a short sale of 100 shares at 50 each?
options: 5,000 — the value received when the shares were sold
10,000 — twice the position size
Unlimited in principle, because the price can rise without any ceiling
Nothing, because the shares were borrowed rather than bought
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The maximum gain is capped at 5,000, which happens if the price reaches zero. The loss has no such limit: at 250 the buy-back costs 25,000 against 5,000 received. The asymmetry that favours a share owner runs against a short seller, and the position can be closed against your will if the lender recalls the shares.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The 5,000 received is the maximum possible gain, not the maximum loss. Buying back is what closes a short, and there is no ceiling on the price you might have to pay — at 250 a share, closing 100 shares costs 25,000.

quiz.question: You invest 10,000, borrow 10,000, and hold 20,000 of shares with a 25% maintenance requirement. How far do the shares have to fall before a margin call?
options: 75%, since the maintenance requirement is 25%
About 33%, at which point the position is worth about 13,333 and your equity is down to 25% of it
50%, because you borrowed half the position
Only a complete loss triggers a call
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Your equity is the position value less the 10,000 loan, so it hits 25% of the position when the position is worth about 13,333 — a fall of roughly 33%. Your own 10,000 is then down to about 3,333, and the broker can sell without waiting for you.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The maintenance requirement applies to your equity as a share of the position, not to the size of the fall. Because the loan stays fixed at 10,000, the call arrives at a position value of about 13,333 — a fall of only around 33%.

quiz.question: A short position of 5,000 carries a borrow fee of 20% a year. If the share price is unchanged after six months, what has happened?
options: Nothing, since the price did not move
The position has cost 500 in borrow fees — 10% of its value — for no price movement at all
The position has gained 500 in interest
The broker must close the position automatically
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Borrow fees accrue whether or not the price moves, so 20% a year on 5,000 costs 500 over six months. A short loses money while nothing happens, which is why being right eventually is not the same as being right in time.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Shorting is not free to hold. The borrow fee is charged for the whole period the position is open — 20% a year on 5,000 is 500 over six months, a 10% loss with the share price completely unchanged.

keyTerms.def: Borrowing from a broker to buy more than your cash allows.
A demand for more collateral; unmet, the broker sells your holdings.
Borrowing and selling shares hoping to buy them back cheaper. Loss is unbounded.

lessons.chapterTitle: Behaviour, Costs and a Written Plan
lessons.title: The Behaviour Gap
lessons.keyIdea: Investors do earn less than the funds they hold, but the most-quoted figures for how much are badly overstated. The gap is real, small, and concentrated in the funds people trade most.

blocks.text: A fund reports a return. The people who owned that fund earned something different. The difference has a name, and it is the most abused statistic in retail investing.
The difference between a fund's published return and the return actually earned by the average unit of money invested in it, caused by money arriving and leaving at different times.

The mechanism is simple and does not require anyone to behave stupidly. A fund's published return assumes you held it for the whole period. Real money does not arrive on day one and sit still. If more money is in the fund during its bad stretches than during its good ones, the average euro earns less than the fund did.
The return of the fund itself, ignoring when money went in or out. This is the number in the fund's marketing material.
The return earned by the actual money invested, weighted by how much was present at each moment. Also called the money-weighted or internal rate of return.
The gap is the second number minus the first. Now the awkward part: almost every figure you will see quoted for it is wrong, and the errors all run in the same direction.

The single most-cited source for this claim is the DALBAR Quantitative Analysis of Investor Behavior, which for years reported gaps of five or six percentage points a year. Wade Pfau, writing in Advisor Perspectives in 2017 under the title A Warning to the Advisory Profession: DALBAR's Math is Wrong, showed that the study compares an investor making ongoing contributions against an index return that assumes a single lump sum invested at the start. Those are two different questions. Michael Kitces has made the same criticism independently. Neither DALBAR figure nor anything derived from it belongs in a serious argument.

Morningstar's Mind the Gap study is a genuine improvement. It uses fund flow data rather than a proxy, and its numbers are far more modest. The 2025 edition reported a gap of about 1.2 percentage points a year over the ten years ending 31 December 2024: investors earned roughly 7.0% a year against the funds' 8.2%, a shortfall Morningstar described as about 15% of the funds' total gains.
That is the figure most careful writers now quote. It is also being contested, by exactly the kind of source this course tells you to go looking for.

Fulkerson, Jordan, Riley and Yan examined the Mind the Gap methodology in a paper titled Bad Timing Does Not Cost Investors 15% of Their Funds' Returns, published in the Financial Analysts Journal in 2026. They identify three mathematical errors in the calculation. Recomputing the 2023 edition's reported 1.7 percentage point gap, they find it should have been 0.03 percentage points. Their estimate of what poor timing actually costs fund investors is around 0.10 percentage points a year — roughly a twelfth of the headline number.
So what should a reader take from this? Not that behaviour does not matter. Something more useful and more precise.
Both studies agree on the pattern even where they disagree on the size. The gap is near zero in broad, boring, automatically-contributed funds. It is largest in the funds people trade actively.

In the 2025 Morningstar data the overall gap was 1.2 points, but international equity funds showed 3.2 points and sector equity funds 2.1 points. Nobody trades a target-date pension fund on a hunch. People do trade a technology sector fund on one.

That is the honest lesson, and it happens to match the direct evidence from Chapter 2. Barber and Odean, in Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth, published in the Journal of Finance in 2000, found that the fifth of households who traded most earned 11.4% a year against a market return of 17.9%. That is a gap of 6.5 points, and it is measured on actual trading accounts rather than inferred from fund flows.
Compounded over 20 years, 10,000 growing at 17.9% becomes about 269,000. The same 10,000 at 11.4% becomes about 87,000. The activity did not cost a slice of the return; it cost most of the outcome.

Put the two findings side by side and the shape is clear. The average fund investor loses very little to timing. The active trader loses a great deal. Averaging those two populations together produces the widely-quoted middling figure that describes neither of them.

Watch what happens when a number is convenient. The large behaviour-gap figures are quoted most enthusiastically by people selling advice, because the gap is the exact size of the value they claim to add. That does not make the number false. It does mean nobody in the chain had a reason to check the arithmetic, and for twenty years nobody did.

The practical conclusion survives all three studies intact. Automatic contributions into broad funds produce almost no gap. Discretionary trading in narrow funds produces a large one. What you hold matters less here than how often you touch it.
The mechanism that produces the gap where it does exist is worth naming, because it is visible while it is happening.
Moving money into a fund after a strong run and out after a weak one, so purchases cluster near highs and sales near lows.

Money flows into a fund after the returns that made it attractive have already happened. The returns being advertised are the ones the earlier holders received. Someone arriving on the strength of those figures owns the fund for the period that follows, which is a different period and often a worse one.

A sector fund returns 40% in a year and attracts large inflows over the following months. The next year it falls 20%. The published two-year record is still positive. The average unit of money in the fund experienced mostly the second year, because most of the money arrived after the first.

Be careful with the phrase the average investor. Both the Morningstar and DALBAR figures describe an average of money, not a typical person. A population where most people do nothing and a small minority trade heavily produces an average that describes neither group. The correct question is not what the average investor loses; it is which of the two groups you are in.

blocks.alt: Three bars comparing estimates of the annual cost of investor timing: the DALBAR figure of about 5 to 6 percentage points, the Morningstar Mind the Gap 2025 figure of 1.2 points, and the Fulkerson, Jordan, Riley and Yan 2026 estimate of about 0.10 points, with panels explaining the methodological objection to each of the first two.

blocks.text: What to look for in your own record. Check whether your purchases cluster after strong periods, which is the honest test of performance chasing. Check whether the funds you trade most are also the narrowest, since that is where every study finds the gap. Check whether your contributions are automatic or discretionary. And treat any advertised return as a statement about the people who owned the fund before you.

List every investment purchase you have made in the last three years with its date. Beside each, note what that holding had done in the twelve months before you bought it. If most purchases followed strong periods, you have measured your own behaviour gap directly, which is more useful than any published average.

quiz.question: The widely-quoted claim that investors lose five or six percentage points a year to bad timing comes mainly from the DALBAR study. What is the main problem with it?
options: DALBAR uses too short a sample period
It compares investors making ongoing contributions against an index return that assumes one lump sum invested at the start — two different questions
The study only covers professional investors
The gap has disappeared since index funds became popular
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Pfau and Kitces independently showed the comparison is not like for like: the investor is contributing over time while the benchmark assumes a single investment at the beginning. Morningstar's better-constructed study puts the gap at 1.2 points, and the 2026 Financial Analysts Journal critique of that study puts the true cost of timing nearer 0.10 points.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The problem is not sample length or coverage. It is that the two returns being subtracted answer different questions — an ongoing-contribution investor is measured against a lump-sum benchmark, so the difference includes far more than timing.

quiz.question: A sector fund returns 40% in one year, attracts large inflows, then falls 20% the next. Why can its published two-year record be positive while most of its investors did badly?
options: Because the published record is calculated incorrectly
Because most of the money arrived after the strong year, so the average unit of money experienced mainly the second year
Because the fund changed its investment strategy between the two years
Because published returns exclude the second year
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The fund's own return assumes you held throughout. The dollar-weighted return reflects when money was actually present, and here most of it arrived after the gains and before the fall. That is the mechanism behind the entire behaviour-gap literature.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The published figure is calculated correctly — it is simply answering a different question. It measures the fund's return over the period, while investors experienced the return of the period they were actually invested for.

quiz.question: Why is the phrase "the average investor loses 1.2 points a year" misleading even when the figure is accurate?
options: Because the figure only applies to professional investors
Because it averages a population where most people do very little and a minority trade heavily, describing neither group
Because behaviour gaps cannot be measured at all
Because the figure is always reported before fees
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Both studies find the gap is near zero in broad automatically-contributed funds and large in narrow actively traded ones. Averaging those two populations produces a number that describes neither. The useful question is which group your own behaviour puts you in.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The figure covers ordinary fund investors and the gap is measurable. The problem is that it is an average across two very different populations — passive contributors with almost no gap, and active traders with a large one.

keyTerms.def: The difference between a fund's return and the return its investors actually earned.
The fund's own return, ignoring when money entered or left.
The return earned by the money actually invested, weighted by when it was present.

lessons.chapterTitle: Behaviour, Costs and a Written Plan
lessons.title: Fees, Taxes and Decades
lessons.keyIdea: A 1% annual fee sounds small and takes about a sixth of a thirty-year pot. Fees are the only input to your result that you know in advance with certainty.

blocks.text: Chapter 1 Lesson 7 introduced the expense ratio and showed that a fee compounds. This lesson does the full arithmetic on a realistic schedule, because the result is larger than almost anyone expects and the numbers are the argument.
Take someone investing 200 a month for 30 years. Assume the underlying market returns 7% a year. Everything below uses that same schedule and differs only in the fee.

Total contributed over the 30 years: 72,000.
With no fee at all, at 7%: about 235,200.
With a 0.20% fee, so 6.8% net: about 226,700.
With a 1.00% fee, so 6.0% net: about 195,900.
With a 2.00% fee, so 5.0% net: about 163,700.
Now state those as what the fee took, rather than what was left.

The 0.20% fee cost about 8,500, or 3.6% of the final pot.
The 1.00% fee cost about 39,400, or 16.7% of the final pot.
The 2.00% fee cost about 71,500, or 30.4% of the final pot — very nearly the entire 72,000 that was contributed.

A 1% fee does not take 1%. Over 30 years it takes about a sixth of everything you end up with. The reason is that the fee is charged on the whole balance every year, including on the growth that previous years' fees already prevented. The gap compounds alongside the portfolio, in the opposite direction.

There is a second way to see the same number, and it is the one worth remembering. A 1% fee on a portfolio expected to return 7% is not one percent of anything meaningful — it is about 14% of your expected return, handed over annually regardless of whether the return arrives.
The cumulative effect of annual charges on a compounding balance. It grows with both the rate charged and the length of time held.

The asymmetry here is the whole point of the lesson. Nobody knows what the market will return over the next 30 years. Everybody can know, today, exactly what they will be charged. One of those two inputs to your final result is uncertain and outside your control. The other is printed on the fact sheet.

The same arithmetic on a single lump sum is just as stark. 10,000 invested for 30 years at 7% becomes about 76,100. At 6% — a one point fee — it becomes about 57,400. The fee cost 18,700, which is nearly twice the amount originally invested.
Fees are not only the expense ratio. Chapter 1 Lesson 7 listed the others, and they are worth restating because they hide in different places.

The expense ratio is deducted inside the fund and never appears on a statement. Trading spreads are paid each time you buy or sell. Platform or custody fees are charged by whoever holds the account. Advice fees, where they apply, sit on top of all of it. Two of these are one-off and two are annual, and only the annual ones compound the way the table above shows.

Three separate 0.5% charges are not a 0.5% cost. Stacked, they behave like the 1.5% line in the table. Add every recurring charge together before comparing anything, because providers rarely present the total in one place.
Taxes work through the same mechanism, with one important difference in how they are triggered.
The reduction in compounding caused by paying tax on gains, dividends or interest along the way rather than at the end.
Tax rules differ by country, and this course will not pretend otherwise or invent a rate to make a tidier example. What transfers everywhere is the structure, and the structure has three parts.

First, tax paid this year on a gain removes not only that amount but every future year of growth on it — the same compounding argument as the fee. Second, in most systems a gain is only taxed when realised, which means selling has a cost that holding does not. Third, most countries offer at least one tax-sheltered account for long-term or retirement savings, and using the available allowance is usually the single highest-value administrative decision available to a small investor.

Find the total annual cost of what you currently hold, or of the fund you are considering. Add the expense ratio, the platform fee and any advice fee. Then look up whether your country offers a tax-sheltered account and what the annual allowance is. Both numbers are knowable today, and together they will move your thirty-year result more than any forecast you will read this year.

This is the least glamorous lesson in the track and probably the most valuable. Nothing else in the course lets you change your expected outcome by a sixth using information that is already public and takes an afternoon to find.
Two practical points follow from the arithmetic, and both are about acting on it rather than admiring it.

The first is that the cost of switching is almost always small next to the cost of not switching. Moving a holding may involve a spread, a transfer charge, and in some cases a tax event. Those are one-off. The fee you are trying to escape is annual, and the table above shows what an annual charge does over a remaining investing life of twenty or thirty years.

The exception is where switching triggers a tax charge you would otherwise never pay, or where you would lose a sheltered wrapper you cannot re-enter. Both are real and both are checkable in advance. Check them, rather than assuming either that switching is free or that it is impossible.
The second point concerns where the largest fees usually hide, which is rarely in the fund.
The full set of recurring charges on a holding: the fund charge, the platform or custody charge, and any advice charge, added together.

A fund at 0.20%, a platform at 0.35% and an advice fee at 0.75% total 1.30% a year. On the schedule in the table above that is close to the 1% line, and it costs roughly a sixth of the final pot. None of the three charges looks large on its own, and no statement adds them up.

blocks.alt: Four bars showing the final value of 200 a month invested for 30 years at an underlying 7 percent, at annual fees of zero, 0.20, 1.00 and 2.00 percent, finishing at about 235,200, 226,700, 195,900 and 163,700.
blocks.caption: A 1 percent fee does not take 1 percent. Over thirty years it takes about a sixth of everything you end up with.

blocks.text: What to look for, in the order that finds the money fastest. Find the platform fee first, because it is the one most people have never looked up. Then the fund charge. Then any advice charge, and ask what it buys, since the answer may well be worth paying for and should still be a decision rather than an inheritance. Then check whether you are using the tax-sheltered allowance available to you, which for most people is worth more than the difference between two index funds.

quiz.question: Someone invests 200 a month for 30 years into a market returning 7% a year. Roughly what proportion of their final pot does a 1% annual fee consume?
options: About 1%, because that is the fee
About 3%, since 1% compounds only slightly
About 17%, because the fee is charged on the whole balance every year and its effect compounds
About 50%, since fees eventually consume most of a long-term portfolio
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The pot is about 235,200 with no fee and about 195,900 at 6% net, so the fee took about 39,400 — roughly 16.7%. The fee is charged annually on the entire balance, including on growth that earlier fees already prevented, so the shortfall compounds alongside the portfolio.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. A 1% annual fee does not cost 1% of the outcome. Charged every year on the whole balance over 30 years, it takes about 39,400 of a 235,200 pot — close to a sixth. Another way to see it: 1% is about 14% of an expected 7% return, paid every year whether the return arrives or not.

quiz.question: A holding carries a 0.20% fund charge, a 0.35% platform charge and a 0.75% advice charge. What is the useful way to think about this?
options: Each charge is small, so the total is not a concern
They stack to 1.30% a year, which over a thirty-year schedule costs close to a sixth of the final pot
Only the fund charge compounds; the others are one-off
The advice charge replaces the other two
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. All three are annual and all three are levied on the whole balance, so they add. At 1.30% the effect is close to the 1% line in the table, which cost about 39,400 of a 235,200 pot. No statement presents that total, which is why it has to be assembled by hand.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. All three are recurring annual charges on the full balance, so they compound together rather than separately or in place of one another. The total of 1.30% is what matters, and over thirty years it takes a large share of the outcome.

quiz.question: Why is the cost of switching to a cheaper fund usually small next to the cost of staying?
options: Because switching is always free
Because switching costs are one-off while the fee difference is annual and compounds over the remaining investing life
Because cheaper funds always outperform expensive ones
Because tax charges never apply to fund switches
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A spread, a transfer charge or a tax event is paid once. The fee is paid every year on the whole balance. The exception worth checking is a switch that triggers a tax charge you would otherwise avoid, or that costs you a sheltered wrapper you cannot re-enter — both are real and both are checkable in advance.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Switching is not always free, and a cheaper fund is not guaranteed to perform better. The argument is purely about timing: one-off costs against an annual charge that compounds for as long as you hold.

keyTerms.def: The compounding effect of annual charges on a growing balance.
The reduction in compounding caused by paying tax on gains along the way.

lessons.chapterTitle: Behaviour, Costs and a Written Plan
lessons.title: Building an Equity Plan
lessons.keyIdea: Decide the sell condition before you buy. A written plan is not a forecast — it is a set of decisions made while you are calm, for use when you are not.

blocks.text: Everything in this track so far has been an input. This lesson turns the inputs into a document, because a decision you have not written down is a decision you will make under pressure.
A short written document setting out what you will hold, in what proportions, how often you will change it, and under what conditions you will sell. Written before investing, consulted during stress.

Forex Chapter 4 Lesson 2 made this argument for trading. It applies with more force to equities, because the holding periods are longer and the moments that test you are years apart. You will not remember your reasoning in 2033. You will be able to read it.
A usable plan answers six questions. Each maps to a lesson you have already read.

One: what is this money for, and when will you need it? Chapter 3 Lesson 1 covered sequence-of-returns risk. Money needed in three years and money needed in thirty are different problems, and the difference is not appetite but arithmetic.
Two: what will you hold? Chapter 2 Lesson 5 gave the honest answer on diversification. Name the funds or the allocation, not a vague intention to be diversified.

Three: how much goes in, and how often? Chapter 3 Lesson 3 distinguished contributing from a salary, which is not a strategy choice, from deploying a sum you already hold, which is. If you are averaging in, the schedule and its end date go in writing here.
Four: what is the maximum any one position may be? Chapter 3 Lesson 2 gave the reason. A limit written in advance is a limit; a limit you decide when a holding is up 300% is a negotiation.
Five: when do you rebalance? This needs its own definition, because it is where most plans quietly fail.
A rule that returns a holding to its target weight only once it drifts beyond a set distance from it — for example, a target of 30% with a band of 5 points, acted on at 25% or 35%.

Bands are better than calendar dates for a practical reason. A fixed annual date makes you trade in years when nothing has drifted, and forbids you from acting in the year when everything has. A band responds to the portfolio rather than to the calendar. Either rule beats no rule, and the choice between them matters far less than writing one down.

Rebalancing feels wrong every single time. It requires selling what has done well to buy what has done badly, which is the opposite of what the recent past appears to recommend. That discomfort is the mechanism working, not a signal that the rule is broken. If it felt comfortable it would not be doing anything.
Six, and the one most plans omit: under what conditions will you sell?

This is the equity version of the invalidation level from Forex Chapter 6 Lesson 2. There, a trade had a price at which the thesis was proven wrong. Here, a holding has a condition — and the condition is almost never a price.

Legitimate written sell conditions: the money is needed for its stated purpose; the holding has drifted outside its rebalancing band; the fund raised its fee; the specific reason you bought a single company no longer holds, such as the business you invested in being sold. Each of these can be checked against fact.

Not a sell condition: it fell a lot and I feel bad. That is a feeling, and feelings are what the document exists to overrule.

Write the plan when nothing is happening. A plan drafted during a 30% drawdown will encode the panic it was meant to prevent, and a plan drafted during a boom will assume the boom continues. The calm moment is the only moment the document is worth writing in, which is exactly why almost nobody writes one until it is too late.

Write the six answers on one page. Date it. Add one line naming what would make you change the plan itself — a genuine change in your circumstances or in the evidence, not a change in the market. Then set a reminder to read it once a year without changing anything. Most of the value comes from the fact that it exists in your own handwriting on a day you were thinking clearly.

Forex Chapter 4 Lesson 2 framed a trading plan around expectancy: the average result of a repeated process, not the outcome of one trade. The equity version of expectancy is a thirty-year contribution schedule. The individual year is noise. The process is the position.
A plan does not need to be long. Here is what a complete one can look like, so the exercise stops being abstract.

Purpose: retirement, not needed for at least 25 years. Holdings: one global equity index fund, 90%; cash held separately, 10%, covering six months of costs. Contributions: 300 a month, automatic, on the first working day. Single-company limit: none, because I hold no single companies. Rebalancing: annually in January, or whenever cash falls below 5% or rises above 15%. Sell conditions: the money is needed for retirement; the fund raises its ongoing charge above 0.30%; the fund is closed or merged. Reviewed each January without changes unless one of the above applies.

That plan is eight lines. It answers every question in this lesson, and its main virtue is that a version of you in a bad year can read it and see that a version of you in a calm year had already considered this.

The most common failure is not a bad plan but a plan that is silent on the situation you actually meet. If your document says nothing about what to do when a holding halves, you will improvise, and the improvisation happens at the worst moment. Where you cannot decide something in advance, write down that you have decided to do nothing, which is itself a rule and a much better one than an unwritten instinct.

blocks.alt: A numbered list of the six questions a written investment plan answers: what the money is for and when it is needed, what will be held, how much goes in and how often, the maximum size of any one position, when to rebalance, and under what conditions to sell.
blocks.caption: Six decisions made while calm, in writing, for use at a moment when you will not be.

blocks.text: What to look for when reviewing your own plan a year later. Check whether you did what it says, and where you did not, whether the deviation improved anything. Check whether any rule turned out to be unusable in practice, since a rule you cannot follow is worse than no rule because it teaches you to ignore the document. And check whether your circumstances have changed, which is the only legitimate reason to change the plan itself.
Two practical points finish the document, and both are about the plan surviving contact with real life.

The first is where it lives. A plan stored only in your own head or in an application you may lose access to is not a plan. Keep it somewhere you will still be able to read in ten years, and keep it in the same place as the list of what you hold and where it is held.

The second is that somebody else should know it exists. If you are the only person who knows what you own and where, then illness or death converts a well-built portfolio into a problem for people who did not choose it. Writing down the institutions, the account types and the location of the plan takes twenty minutes and is the most neglected item in personal investing.

quiz.question: Why does a written plan specify sell conditions before the first purchase rather than when a holding falls?
options: Because selling is always a mistake and the plan is there to prevent it
Because a condition decided while calm can be checked against fact, whereas one decided during a fall is a reaction to the fall itself
Because tax rules require a stated sell condition in advance
Because sell conditions must be set at a specific price to be valid
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The document exists to move the decision from the stressed moment to the calm one. A written condition — the money is needed, the band was breached, the fee rose, the reason for buying no longer holds — is checkable. A decision made mid-drawdown is a response to how the drawdown feels, which is the thing the plan is meant to overrule.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The point is not that selling is wrong, nor that the condition must be a price — for equities it usually is not. It is that a condition written while calm can be tested against fact, while one invented during a fall is driven by the fall.

quiz.question: A plan is silent on what to do when a holding halves in value. Why is this the most common failure mode?
options: Because regulators require the scenario to be documented
Because the investor will improvise at exactly the moment they are least able to think clearly
Because a halving is the most likely outcome for any holding
Because plans must specify a price for every holding
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A gap in the document is filled in the moment, and the moment is a drawdown. Where a decision genuinely cannot be made in advance, the right entry is that you have decided to do nothing — that is still a rule, and it is far better than an unwritten instinct.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Nothing requires the scenario to be documented and a halving is not the expected outcome. The problem is that an unwritten decision gets made under stress, which is precisely what the document exists to prevent.

quiz.question: Reviewing a plan a year later, you find you followed a rule that turned out to be impractical. What does that indicate?
options: The plan was correct and the circumstances were wrong
A rule you cannot follow in practice is worse than no rule, because it trains you to ignore the document — so the rule should be rewritten
Plans should never be changed once written
The rule should be kept and applied more strictly next year
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The document only works if it is followed, so an unusable rule damages the whole plan by teaching you that its contents are optional. Rewrite it into something you will actually do. That is a different thing from abandoning a rule because the market moved against it.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Plans are meant to be revised when the revision is justified by your circumstances or by a rule proving unworkable. What is not a reason to revise is the market having done something uncomfortable.

keyTerms.def: A short written document setting out holdings, contributions, limits and sell conditions.
A rule to restore a target weight once drift exceeds a set distance.

lessons.title: The Dot-Com Bubble (1995–2002)
lessons.keyIdea: The Nasdaq Composite fell 78% and took fifteen years to regain its peak. Recovery is a fact about indexes; whether it is a fact about you depends on how long you had.

blocks.text: The claim that stocks always recover is true of the indexes usually quoted and much less useful than it sounds. This case study puts real dates and real numbers on the word recover.

Through the late 1990s, companies with internet business models attracted valuations that could not be justified by cash flows, because most had none. Chapter 2 Lesson 2 explained that a multiple is a compressed forecast. In 1999 the forecast being compressed was that revenue would arrive later and be enormous.
Pricing an asset on a story about its future rather than on observable cash flows. Not always wrong, but unfalsifiable while the story lasts.
Here is what happened to the index that concentrated those companies.

The Nasdaq Composite closed at its peak of 5,048.62 on 10 March 2000.
It reached its trough at 1,114.11 on 9 October 2002.
That is a fall of 77.9%.
It next closed above the 2000 peak on 23 April 2015, at 5,056.06.
The round trip took 15 years, 1 month and 13 days.
Chapter 3 Lesson 2 gave the recovery arithmetic. Applied here it is brutal.

A 77.9% fall requires a gain of about 353% simply to return to where it started. Not 78%. The percentages are taken from different bases: the fall is measured from the peak, the recovery from the trough.

Fifteen years is not an abstraction. Someone who bought the index in March 2000 at age 55 was 70 before the position was worth what they paid, in nominal terms and before inflation. The statement that the market recovered is true and was no help to them. Recovery is a property of the index; whether it reaches you depends on your time horizon, which is exactly the sequence-of-returns risk from Chapter 3 Lesson 1.
Two further points are worth extracting, because both recur.

First, the index was not the whole market. The broad S&P 500 fell substantially less over the same period, and a globally diversified holding fell less still. The Nasdaq Composite was heavily weighted toward exactly the companies in the story. Chapter 1 Lesson 4 said an index measures a chosen basket; in 2000 the chosen basket was the bubble.

Second, many of the individual companies never recovered at all. The index regained its level partly because its failed constituents were removed and replaced by survivors. An index recovers by composition in a way a portfolio of the original companies could not.

This is survivorship at the index level, and it is why the roadmap for this track flagged stocks always go up over twenty years as a claim needing the same scrutiny as any other. The sentence is usually true of a continuously reconstituted index. It was not true of Pets.com, and an index is not a promise made to any particular holding.
What would have helped? Nothing in this course would have told anyone when the peak was. Several things would have limited the damage.

A position size that survived a 78% fall in one holding, from Chapter 3 Lesson 2. Diversification beyond a single concentrated index, from Chapter 2 Lesson 5. Continued contributions through the fall, which bought the trough. And a written sell condition, from the previous lesson, so that the decision to hold was a decision rather than a paralysis.

The reader who kept contributing monthly from 2000 through 2002 did not need the index to reach 5,048 to be whole. Their average purchase price was far below the peak. That is not a consolation prize — it is the mechanical reason a contribution schedule survives a drawdown that a lump sum at the top does not.
The uncomfortable part of this case study is that narrative valuation is only obvious afterwards. It is worth being precise about what could and could not have been seen at the time.

What was visible in 1999: companies with no earnings valued at large multiples of revenue, index concentration rising, and a widely repeated argument that traditional valuation no longer applied to a new kind of business. What was not visible: when it would end, or which of the companies would survive and become genuinely enormous. Both of those questions were answered, and some of the survivors did justify remarkable valuations.

That is why this is not a lesson about spotting bubbles. Anyone who exited in 1997 on valuation grounds was right about the valuation and missed three more years of gains, and anyone who dismissed the entire sector missed the companies that went on to dominate the following two decades. The defence being taught here is position sizing and diversification, which work without requiring you to call the top.

blocks.text: What to look for when a similar argument appears, as it does regularly. Notice when valuation is being dismissed rather than argued — the phrase this time the old measures do not apply is the specific signal, and it is not always wrong, which is what makes it dangerous. Notice when an index's top ten holdings become an unusually large share of the whole. Notice when the case for owning something rests entirely on what it might become. And check what proportion of your own portfolio depends on the same story being true.

Look up the combined weight of the ten largest companies in the main index you are exposed to, and what proportion of them share a single industry. Then write down what your portfolio would do if that industry fell 50% while everything else was flat. You are not predicting anything. You are measuring an exposure you already hold.
The most durable lesson is one people resist, because it separates two judgements that feel like the same judgement.

Almost every prediction made in 1999 about what the internet would become turned out to be correct, and often understated. Being right about the technology was not the same as being right about the price, because the price already contained the prediction. Chapter 2 Lesson 2 made this point in the abstract; the bubble is the point demonstrated at scale.

Whenever you find yourself certain about a technology, a trend or an industry, ask the separate question of what is already in the price. Being correct about the future and losing money are entirely compatible states, and they were the normal experience of the people who bought the right sector at the wrong level.

quiz.question: The Nasdaq Composite fell 77.9% from its March 2000 peak. What gain from the trough was needed to get back to that peak, and how long did it take?
options: About 78%, and around three years
About 130%, and around eight years
About 353%, and just over fifteen years
About 200%, and around ten years
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The fall and the recovery are measured from different bases: recovering from a 77.9% fall requires a gain of about 353%. The index closed at 1,114.11 on 9 October 2002 and did not close above the March 2000 peak until 23 April 2015 — fifteen years and one month later.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. A fall of 77.9% is measured from the peak; the recovery is measured from the much smaller trough, so it needs about 353%, not 78%. The index took until 23 April 2015 to regain its 10 March 2000 peak.

quiz.question: What is the main defence this case study teaches against an episode like the dot-com bubble?
options: Learning to identify bubbles early and exit before they burst
Position sizing and diversification, which limit the damage without requiring anyone to call the top
Avoiding technology companies entirely
Holding only companies with low P/E ratios
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Anyone exiting on valuation grounds in 1997 was right about the valuation and missed three more years of gains, and anyone dismissing the sector entirely missed the companies that went on to dominate. Sizing and diversification work without requiring a forecast, which is why they are the defence being taught.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Identifying the top reliably is exactly what nobody managed, and avoiding the sector meant missing its eventual winners. The defence that works without a forecast is limiting how much any single story can cost you.

quiz.question: Why did the Nasdaq Composite regain its level partly through a mechanism a portfolio of the original companies could not use?
options: Because index levels are adjusted for inflation
Because failed constituents were removed from the index and replaced by survivors, so the index recovered by composition
Because the index switched to price weighting
Because dividends were added back into the index
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. An index is continuously reconstituted, so companies that failed left it and were replaced. A holder of the original 2000 constituents had no such mechanism. This is survivorship at the index level, and it is why "the market always recovers" is a weaker claim than it sounds.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The recovery was not an accounting adjustment or a change of weighting method. The index replaced its failures with survivors over the intervening years — something an unchanged portfolio of the original companies could not do.

keyTerms.def: Pricing an asset on a story about its future rather than on observable cash flows.

lessons.title: 2007–2009 and the Shape of a Recovery
lessons.keyIdea: The S&P 500 fell 57% and regained its peak in five and a half years. The investor who kept contributing and the one who stopped ended the same period in different worlds.

blocks.text: The previous lesson showed a fifteen-year recovery. This one shows a five-and-a-half-year recovery of almost the same depth, which is the point: the depth of a fall tells you very little about how long it lasts.

The S&P 500 closed at its pre-crisis peak of 1,565.15 on 9 October 2007.
It closed at its trough of 676.53 on 9 March 2009.
That is a fall of 56.8%, and required a gain of about 131% to recover.
It closed at a new all-time high on 28 March 2013, at about 1,569.
The round trip took approximately five and a half years.

Set that beside the Nasdaq: a 78% fall took fifteen years, a 57% fall took five and a half. The relationship between how far a market falls and how long it takes to come back is not reliable enough to plan around, which is why Chapter 3 Lesson 1 insisted on treating drawdown depth and drawdown duration as two separate risks.
The time from a peak to the recovery of that peak, as distinct from the depth of the fall in between.
Now the part that matters more than either figure. Two investors lived through this period identically until early 2009, and then made different decisions.

Both had been contributing monthly since 2005. Both watched the balance fall by more than half.

The first kept contributing through 2008 and 2009. Every contribution from October 2008 to mid-2010 bought at prices well below the 2007 peak, and the March 2009 contributions bought near the lowest prices of the entire period.

The second stopped contributing in November 2008, when it had become obvious that things were getting worse, and resumed in 2013 when the market had recovered and it felt safe again.

The second investor was not irrational. Stopping felt like risk management, and in November 2008 there was no way to know the trough was four months away. But the decision had a specific and permanent cost: it converted the entire cheap period into a period of no purchases, and then resumed buying only after prices had doubled.

The second investor did not sell. That is the point worth sitting with. They simply stopped buying, which felt like caution rather than a transaction, and it cost them the best purchase prices in a decade. A pause in contributions is a decision with the same consequences as a sale of the amount you would have bought — it just does not feel like one, because nothing appears on the statement.

Chapter 3 Lesson 3 said averaging in is a behavioural tool with a real cost. This is the same idea running the other way. The mechanical value of a contribution schedule is that it buys most units when prices are lowest, and that value only exists if the schedule is not interrupted precisely when prices are lowest.
Sequence-of-returns risk cuts differently depending on which end of the plan you are at.

A young investor contributing into a crash is being handed cheap assets over years, and the crash is close to a gift. A retiree drawing income during the same crash is selling units at the bottom to pay for living costs, permanently removing them from the recovery. The market did one thing. It did opposite things to two people.
This is why the first question in the previous lesson's plan is when will you need this money. It is not a preliminary. It changes the sign of the answer.

One more observation about the recovery itself. Its shape was uneven and concentrated. Large single-day and single-week gains clustered inside the most frightening weeks, near the March 2009 trough. Anyone who moved to cash after the worst of the falls and waited for clarity was out of the market during precisely the days that produced the recovery.

That is not an argument that you must never hold cash. It is the reason the decision belongs in a document written in advance, checked against a condition, rather than made on a Tuesday in March when the news is at its worst.
One further comparison makes the sequence risk concrete, because the same market did opposite things to two people at different stages.

Two people held identical portfolios in October 2007. The first was 30 and contributing. Over the next five and a half years they bought continuously at prices below the 2007 peak, and by March 2013 held far more units than they started with, at a level that had fully recovered. The second was 65 and withdrawing 4% a year for living costs. Every withdrawal between 2008 and 2011 sold units at depressed prices, and those units were not there to participate in the recovery.

Neither person made a mistake, and their average return over the period was identical. The order in which the returns arrived, combined with which direction their money was flowing, produced entirely different outcomes. That is sequence-of-returns risk in one paragraph.

The practical implication is uncomfortable and worth stating anyway. The closer you are to needing the money, the less an equity holding is a long-term investment and the more it is a bet on a specific decade. That is not an argument against holding equities near retirement; it is an argument for holding something else alongside them, so the withdrawals do not have to come from the fallen asset.

blocks.caption: Identical portfolios and identical average returns. What differed was the direction their money was flowing.

blocks.text: What to look for in your own position. Establish whether money is flowing into your portfolio or out of it, because that single fact reverses the meaning of a fall. Establish how many years of withdrawals you could cover without selling equities. Check whether your contribution schedule is automatic, since automatic schedules are the ones that survive a crisis. And decide now, in writing, what would make you stop contributing — the honest answer for most readers should be a change in income, not a change in prices.

Write down what you contributed, or withdrew, in each of the last three years. Then write what you would do if the market fell 40% next month and stayed down for three years. If your answer involves reducing contributions, note that this is the decision the second investor in this lesson made, and it cost them the cheapest prices of the decade.
There is one action available during a fall of this kind that is neither buying more nor selling, and it is the one a written plan makes possible.

An investor holding both equities and cash finds their equity weight has dropped sharply after a large fall, purely because equities fell and cash did not. A rebalancing rule moves money from cash into equities to restore the intended weights, which means buying at depressed prices without any judgement about the bottom being required.

That action is close to unbearable in the moment and it is why the rule has to exist in writing beforehand. Chapter 4 Lesson 3 makes the same point in the abstract. In March 2009 the abstract version and the lived version were very far apart, and only the people with the rule already written found the decision available to them.

quiz.question: An investor contributing monthly stopped their contributions in November 2008 and resumed in 2013, without ever selling. What was the main cost of that decision?
options: None, since they never sold and so never realised a loss
They missed the period of lowest prices — including the March 2009 trough — and resumed buying only after prices had roughly doubled
They incurred additional trading fees when they resumed
They lost the dividends on shares they already held
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Pausing contributions is a decision with the same effect as declining to buy at the bottom, even though nothing appears on the statement. The S&P 500 troughed at 676.53 on 9 March 2009 and had regained roughly 1,569 by March 2013, so the resumed contributions bought at more than twice the price the paused ones would have.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. They never sold, so the harm is not a realised loss and it is not fees or dividends. The cost is the purchases they did not make: the pause covered exactly the cheapest prices of the period, and buying resumed only after the market had roughly doubled off the trough.

quiz.question: Two investors held identical portfolios through 2007 to 2013 and experienced identical average returns. One was contributing, the other withdrawing 4% a year. Why did they end in very different positions?
options: Because the withdrawing investor held riskier assets
Because the direction of their cash flow reversed the meaning of the fall — contributions bought depressed prices while withdrawals sold them
Because average returns are not a meaningful measure
Because the contributing investor timed the market better
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The same sequence of returns helps someone buying and harms someone selling. Units sold at depressed prices between 2008 and 2011 were not there for the recovery, while units bought in the same period were. Neither investor made an error, which is what makes sequence risk a structural rather than a behavioural problem.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The portfolios and the average returns were identical and neither investor timed anything. What differed was the direction their money was flowing, which determines whether a fall hands you cheap assets or forces you to sell at a discount.

quiz.question: What follows from the observation that a large part of the post-2009 recovery came in concentrated bursts near the trough?
options: That investors should trade more actively during volatile periods
That moving to cash and waiting for clarity tends to miss precisely the days that produce the recovery, which is why the decision belongs in a written rule
That the recovery was artificial
That equity markets always recover within five years
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The strongest days clustered inside the most frightening weeks, so waiting for conditions to look safe meant being absent for the recovery. That is not an argument that cash is never appropriate — it is an argument for deciding the rule in advance rather than during the week the news is at its worst.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The point is not to trade more, and no general rule about five-year recoveries follows — the previous lesson showed a fifteen-year one. It is that the recovery's best days sat inside its worst weeks, which punishes decisions made for the sake of clarity.

keyTerms.def: The time from a peak to the recovery of that peak, distinct from the depth of the fall.

lessons.title: GameStop, January 2021
lessons.keyIdea: The regulator investigated the most repeated explanation of the episode and concluded it was not what happened. The real story was in the settlement plumbing.

blocks.text: In January 2021 the shares of GameStop, a struggling retailer of video games, rose by a very large multiple within days and then collapsed. Almost everyone can tell you why. The regulator looked, and found the popular explanation does not hold.
Start with the mechanisms, because two of them are genuinely important and Chapter 3 Lesson 4 introduced the first.
A rise driven by short sellers being forced to buy back shares to close their positions, whose buying pushes the price higher, forcing more shorts to buy.
A rise driven by dealers who sold call options buying the underlying shares to hedge their exposure, buying more as the price rises.

One fact about GameStop is not in dispute and is genuinely extraordinary. More than 100% of the company's freely tradable shares had been sold short — possible because a borrowed share, once sold, can be borrowed and sold again by its new owner. The United States Securities and Exchange Commission noted in its review that GameStop was the only one of the so-called meme stocks where this was true.
So the short squeeze explanation had the strongest possible starting evidence. Here is what the regulator concluded anyway.

The SEC published its Staff Report on Equity and Options Market Structure Conditions in Early 2021 on 18 October 2021. Examining the trade and order data directly, staff found that the price rise was driven mainly by buying from investors who did not hold short positions, and that short covering peaked and declined before the price reached its highest levels. The report concluded that neither a short squeeze nor a gamma squeeze was the primary cause of the rise. The explanation everyone repeats is the one the data does not support.

This is the clearest example in the entire course of the thread the course keeps returning to. A story can be vivid, mechanically plausible, universally repeated, told by people who were there, and still wrong. What separated the story from the fact was that someone had the order data and looked.

The report is not beyond challenge either, and the honest position is to say so. Academic work has since disputed parts of its analysis and argued that short covering played a larger role than staff concluded. The useful state of knowledge is a genuine disagreement between people examining data, not the confident version repeated on either side.
The part of the episode that is settled, and that most retellings skip, is the plumbing.

On 28 January 2021 several brokerages restricted buying in GameStop and other affected shares. Customers could sell but not buy. This was widely read as brokers protecting hedge funds, and the real explanation is duller and more instructive.
Collateral a broker must post to the central clearing house to cover the risk of trades between execution and settlement.

Chapter 1 Lesson 3 covered settlement, and noted that a trade takes time to complete. During that window the clearing house carries the risk that one side fails, and it demands collateral in proportion to the volatility and volume of what is pending. In late January 2021 both were extreme, and the collateral demands on brokers rose by amounts they had to meet within hours.
Restricting buying reduced the pending obligations that had to be collateralised. Selling did not, which is why one direction was blocked and the other was not.

Note what this means for a retail investor. You could hold a share, be entirely correct about it, and be prevented from acting by a collateral rule between two institutions you have never heard of and have no relationship with. That is a real risk and it is not in any valuation model. It is also a large part of why the United States moved to a shorter settlement cycle in May 2024, as Chapter 1 Lesson 3 noted — less time between trade and settlement means less risk to collateralise.

Three things to carry forward. Position sizing, from Chapter 3 Lesson 2, is the only defence against an instrument that can move like this in either direction. The unbounded loss on a short, from Chapter 3 Lesson 4, was demonstrated live and at scale. And the most confidently repeated explanation of a famous market event was checked against the order data by the people who have it, and did not survive.
It is worth separating what this episode is usually taken to prove from what it can actually support, because both sides drew conclusions the evidence does not carry.

It does not show that coordinated retail buyers can reliably defeat professional investors, since the regulator found the rise was not primarily a squeeze and the price collapsed afterwards. It does not show that the restrictions were a conspiracy, since the collateral mechanism is documented and applied to brokers rather than to any particular customer. And it does not show that short selling is illegitimate, though it does show what more than 100% of a float being sold short can do to the people on that side.

What it does show, unambiguously, is that the story that reaches you and the story in the data can be different, and that almost nobody checks. The SEC report has been publicly available since October 2021. The explanation it does not support remains the one most commonly repeated, five years later, including by people who are certain about it.
