blocks.text: What to look for when a market event becomes a story. Find out whether a regulator or exchange published an examination of it, since these exist more often than people expect and are usually free. Notice whether the popular explanation was formed before or after any data was available — for this episode it was formed within days, and the data took nine months. Ask who benefits from each version of the story. And keep the mechanism separate from the narrative: the settlement plumbing explains the restrictions completely, and it is the part of the episode nobody had a motive to publicise.

Take any market event you believe you understand and find the primary document about it — a regulator's report, an exchange notice, or a company filing. Read the summary. Then compare it with the version you held. This is the single habit that separates the course's method from the commentary that surrounds it, and it costs an hour.
One further mechanism deserves attention because it was how many participants actually took part.

Buying call options gives leveraged exposure to a rise for a small outlay, with the loss capped at the premium paid. That capped loss makes it feel safer than margin, and in one narrow sense it is. What it hides is that the option expires: the position can be entirely correct about the direction and still expire worthless because the move happened a week late.

An instrument where you can be right about the company, right about the direction, and still lose everything you put in is not a beginner's instrument, whatever its maximum loss. This track does not teach options, and the reason is not that they are exotic — it is that they add a deadline to a discipline that already struggles with patience.

quiz.question: What did the SEC staff report of October 2021 conclude about the cause of GameStop's price rise?
options: That a short squeeze was the primary cause, as commonly believed
That a gamma squeeze in call options was the primary cause
That neither a short nor a gamma squeeze was the primary cause — buying came mainly from investors without short positions, and short covering peaked before the highest prices
That the rise was caused entirely by the brokerage trading restrictions
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Examining the order and trade data, staff found the rise was driven mainly by buyers who held no short positions, and that short covering peaked and fell away before the price peaked. GameStop genuinely did have more than 100% of its float sold short — the strongest possible circumstantial case — and the data still did not support the squeeze explanation. Some academic work disputes parts of the report, so the honest summary is an open disagreement rather than a settled answer either way.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. That is the popular explanation, and it is the one the regulator examined and did not find support for. Buying came mainly from investors with no short positions, and short covering peaked before the price did — despite GameStop being the one meme stock with over 100% of its float sold short.

quiz.question: Why did brokerages allow customers to sell GameStop shares but not buy them on 28 January 2021?
options: They were instructed to protect hedge funds with short positions
Restricting buying reduced the pending obligations they had to post collateral against at the clearing house, while selling did not
The exchange had suspended new purchases market-wide
They had run out of shares to sell to customers
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Collateral demands rise with the volatility and volume of trades awaiting settlement, and in late January 2021 both were extreme. Restricting purchases reduced the obligations requiring collateral; sales did not. This is also part of why the United States shortened its settlement cycle in May 2024.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The asymmetry follows from the clearing mechanism rather than from any instruction. Pending purchases created obligations the broker had to collateralise within hours; sales did not create the same demand, so only one direction was restricted.

quiz.question: What is the most defensible summary of what the GameStop episode established?
options: That coordinated retail buyers can reliably defeat professional investors
That the popular explanation of a famous market event went unchecked against publicly available data for years, and that settlement plumbing can prevent you from acting
That short selling should be prohibited
That the SEC report settled every question about the episode
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The price collapsed afterwards, so no reliable defeat of professionals was demonstrated. The report itself is contested by later academic work, so it did not settle everything. What is solid is that the common explanation is unsupported by the order data, and that a collateral rule between institutions can stop a correct investor from trading.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The rise did not persist, the report has itself been challenged in academic work, and nothing here argues for prohibiting short selling. The durable lessons are about unchecked narratives and about the plumbing that can prevent you from acting.

keyTerms.def: A rise driven by short sellers being forced to buy back shares.
A rise driven by option dealers hedging by buying the underlying shares.
Collateral a broker posts to the clearing house to cover risk before settlement.

lessons.title: The Six-Pillar Thesis, Adapted for Equities
lessons.keyIdea: The same six pillars transfer from currencies to shares, but a share has cash flows, so valuation stops being relative and becomes an estimate you can be wrong about in a specific way.

blocks.text: Forex Chapter 6 Lesson 1 replaced a strong feeling with a written thesis scored against six pillars. The structure transfers to equities. What each pillar means does not, and the differences are where the work is.
A written, structured argument for why a specific position should work, built from several independent lines of evidence rather than one opinion.
The six pillars are fundamentals, valuation, catalyst, positioning and sentiment, momentum, and carry. Take each in its equity form.

Fundamentals. In currencies this means growth, inflation and policy — economy-level data nobody controls. In equities it means the three statements from Chapter 2 Lesson 1, produced by the company being assessed, audited but not neutral. The information is far richer and its source has an interest in how it looks. Cash flow is the statement hardest to dress up, which is why that lesson gave it the most weight.

Valuation. This is the pillar that changes most. A currency has no cash flows, so valuation is always relative — one currency against another, or against its own history. A share has cash flows, so its price implies a specific forecast. Chapter 2 Lesson 2 made the point that a multiple is a compressed forecast; the thesis version is to decompress it and state which part of the forecast you disagree with.

A weak thesis says the shares are cheap at 11 times earnings. A usable one says the price implies earnings decline about 5% a year indefinitely; the order book and the contract renewals suggest flat earnings; if earnings are merely flat the multiple is unjustifiably low, and here is what I expect to see in the next two reports if I am right.

Decompressing the forecast is what makes the thesis falsifiable. Cheap is an opinion and cannot be wrong on a date. The market expects a 5% annual decline and I expect flat can be wrong, visibly, at the next set of results. Only the second kind of claim can teach you anything.

Catalyst. Currencies wait on policy meetings and data releases. Equities have a denser and more predictable calendar: results dates, index inclusions, regulatory decisions, contract awards, product launches. The advantage is that the date is often known in advance. The trap is the same as in Forex — a thesis with no reason to move now is a reason to wait, not to buy.

Positioning and sentiment. In currencies this comes from futures positioning data. In equities the closest equivalents are short interest, fund flows and analyst estimate revisions. Chapter 5 gave both the reason to watch it and the reason not to trust a simple reading of it: GameStop had the most extreme short interest anywhere, and the regulator still found short covering was not what drove the price.
Momentum. This pillar has the strongest evidence behind it in equities specifically, and it is worth naming the source.

Jegadeesh and Titman, in Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers, published in the Journal of Finance in 1993, found that buying stocks that had performed well over the previous three to twelve months and selling those that had performed badly produced significant positive returns over similar holding periods. They also found that part of the abnormal return dissipated over the following two years — the effect is real and it is not permanent.

Asness, Moskowitz and Pedersen, in Value and Momentum Everywhere, published in the Journal of Finance in 2013, found both value and momentum premia across eight different markets and asset classes, and — the finding that matters for a thesis — that value and momentum are negatively correlated with each other. Two pillars that disagree are not a contradiction. They are the reason to hold both.

That negative correlation is why the value pillar and the momentum pillar so often point opposite ways. A cheap share is usually cheap because it has been falling. When valuation and momentum both point the same way, that is genuinely rare and worth noticing — but check first that they are two independent readings rather than the same story counted twice.

Carry. In currencies, carry is the interest rate differential. In equities the nearest equivalent is what the holding pays you while you wait: the dividend yield, or more completely the shareholder yield including buybacks. Chapter 1 Lesson 6 established that a dividend is not free money, since the price drops by roughly the payment. Carry here means the return that does not require the market to agree with you, which is a different and more modest claim.
No single pillar is a position. That was true in Forex and it is true here. Conviction means how many independent pillars agree, and the emphasis belongs on independent.

There is evidence that conviction defined this way pays. Antón, Cohen and Polk, in their paper Best Ideas, found that the stocks in which professional managers show the most ex-ante conviction outperformed both the market and those same managers' other holdings by roughly 2.8 to 4.5% a year, while the rest of what they held did not beat the market at all.

Read that finding precisely, because it is easy to misuse. It does not say confidence produces returns. It says a manager's single best-analysed idea is where their edge is concentrated, and everything else they own dilutes it. The six pillars are a method for finding out which of your ideas that is — and for most readers of this track the honest answer will be that no idea clears the bar, which is a legitimate result that Chapter 2 Lesson 4 already prepared you for.
Scoring the pillars is what turns the framework from a checklist into a decision, and the scoring has to be honest about independence.

A worked mini-thesis. Fundamentals: revenue flat for three years, operating cash flow stable, free cash flow positive, no net debt — one pillar, weakly supportive. Valuation: trading at 9 times earnings against its own ten-year average of 15, implying a decline the order book does not show — supportive. Catalyst: a contract renewal decision due within four months — supportive, with a date. Positioning: short interest low, no unusual flows — neutral. Momentum: the shares have fallen 30% over twelve months — actively against. Carry: a 4% dividend covered twice by earnings — supportive.

That is four supportive pillars, one neutral, one against, and a dated catalyst. It is a genuine thesis. Note that momentum disagrees, which the previous section said to expect: cheap shares are usually cheap because they have been falling, and the two pillars are negatively correlated by construction.

The most common error in scoring is counting one story as several pillars. If the valuation is low because the shares fell, and the dividend yield is high because the shares fell, and the sentiment is poor because the shares fell, that is one observation recorded three times. Independence is the entire source of the framework's value, and it is what makes the exercise harder than it looks.

blocks.alt: Six scored bars for a worked equity thesis: fundamentals weakly supportive, valuation supportive at 9 times earnings against a ten-year average of 15, a dated catalyst supportive, positioning neutral, momentum against after a 30 percent fall, and carry supportive on a covered 4 percent dividend.
blocks.caption: Conviction means how many independent pillars agree. Independent is the word doing the work.

blocks.text: What to look for before acting on any thesis, your own or someone else's. Check that each pillar rests on a different piece of evidence. Check that at least one has a date attached, since a thesis with no catalyst is a reason to wait. Write down what would falsify the valuation claim specifically, because that is the pillar most likely to be an opinion in disguise. And confirm that the position size would be acceptable if every pillar turned out to be wrong at once, which happens.

Take any company you have considered buying and score all six pillars in writing, with one sentence of evidence for each. Then cross out any pillar that rests on the same underlying fact as another. Most first attempts lose two or three pillars at this step, and the remaining count is the honest strength of the case.

quiz.question: What is the main way the valuation pillar differs between currencies and shares?
options: Valuation does not apply to shares at all, only to currencies
A share has cash flows, so its price implies a specific forecast that can be stated and disagreed with; a currency has none, so its valuation is always relative
Share valuation is objective while currency valuation is subjective
Currencies are valued on cash flows and shares on sentiment
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. That is what makes an equity thesis falsifiable. Saying the shares are cheap is an opinion that cannot be wrong on a date. Saying the price implies a 5% annual earnings decline while I expect flat earnings is a claim the next set of results can contradict — and only that kind of claim teaches you anything.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Both are valued, and neither is purely objective. The difference is that a share has cash flows, so its price contains an implied forecast you can decompress and disagree with specifically. A currency has no cash flows, so its valuation can only ever be relative to another currency or to its own history.

quiz.question: A thesis records a low valuation, a high dividend yield and poor sentiment as three supporting pillars, all of which follow from the share price having fallen. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — three pillars agree, which is a strong thesis
It is one observation counted three times, and independence is the entire source of the framework's value
Dividend yield is not one of the six pillars
Sentiment should never be counted as supportive
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Conviction comes from independent evidence agreeing, not from restating one fact in three vocabularies. A falling price mechanically lowers the multiple and raises the yield, so all three readings carry the same information — and the thesis is weaker than the count suggests.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Carry, expressed as dividend or shareholder yield, is a legitimate pillar, and sentiment can genuinely support a case. The failure here is that all three readings derive from the same event, so they are not independent evidence.

quiz.question: A thesis has four supportive pillars but momentum points firmly the other way. What does the factor evidence suggest about this?
options: The thesis should be abandoned, since momentum overrides valuation
This is expected — value and momentum are negatively correlated, so a cheap share is usually one that has been falling
Momentum is not relevant to individual companies
The four supportive pillars must be miscounted
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Asness, Moskowitz and Pedersen found value and momentum to be negatively correlated within and across asset classes, which is why the two pillars so often disagree. That disagreement is the reason to consider both rather than a reason to discard either, and when they do align it is genuinely unusual.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Momentum is well documented for individual shares, and neither pillar overrides the other. Their disagreement here is the normal case: cheapness usually arises from a falling price, which is exactly what negative momentum measures.

keyTerms.def: A written argument for a position built from several independent lines of evidence.
What a holding returns to owners through dividends and buybacks combined — the equity form of carry.

lessons.title: Regime Mapping for Equities
lessons.keyIdea: Equities sit near the end of the transmission chain, so the information that moves them usually arrives somewhere else first. Reading the regime tells you which pillar will work — and sometimes that the answer is none.

blocks.text: A professional does not look for positions everywhere at once. They first ask what kind of market this is, because the answer decides which of the six pillars has any power in it.
The prevailing environment: whether risk appetite is rising or falling, whether volatility is low or high, and whether prices are trending or ranging.
Forex Chapter 6 Lesson 3 introduced the transmission chain. It is worth restating with equities placed on it correctly, because their position explains most of what feels unpredictable about them.
The path by which a change in monetary policy moves across markets: interest rates first, then currencies and bonds, then credit and equities, then commodities and other risk assets.

Equities are late on that chain, and that has a specific consequence. By the time a policy change is visible in share prices, it has usually already appeared in rates and in credit. Someone watching only equities is reading the last link and calling it news.

A central bank signals higher rates for longer. Government bond yields move first. Currencies adjust. Corporate credit spreads widen as borrowing becomes more expensive. Only then do equity prices reflect it — through two separate channels, since higher rates raise the discount applied to future cash flows and also slow the economy those cash flows come from.

That double channel is why long-duration shares — companies whose value depends on profits far in the future — move most when rates move. It is the same arithmetic as Chapter 2 Lesson 2. A high multiple is a bet on distant cash flows, and distant cash flows are exactly what a higher discount rate reduces most.
Three regimes cover most of what a reader will meet, and each favours a different pillar.

A calm trending regime, with low volatility and rising risk appetite, is where momentum works. Jegadeesh and Titman's effect from the previous lesson lives here. Valuation is at its least useful, because cheap things stay cheap while the trend continues.

A stressed regime, with high volatility and falling risk appetite, is where correlations converge and diversification does least. Momentum reverses violently. Valuation begins to matter again, but only for someone with the time horizon to wait for it to be recognised.
A ranging regime, with no clear trend and no imminent catalyst, is where most forced positions are taken and most edges are given back.
A market with no clear trend, no imminent catalyst and no pillar strongly aligned. The correct position is often none.

For an equity investor the no-trade regime does not mean sell everything. A long-term contribution schedule is not a position taken on a regime, and stopping it on a regime read is exactly the error Chapter 5 Lesson 2 documented. No-trade applies to discretionary additions: the single company you were about to buy because the story is good and nothing else is happening.
Two honest limits on all of this, because the course does not sell certainty.

First, regimes are named confidently in hindsight and are ambiguous while you are inside them. Nobody rang a bell in March 2009. The value of regime mapping is not that it calls turns; it is that it stops you applying a momentum thesis in a market that has stopped trending.

Second, Chapter 2 Lesson 4 covered market efficiency, and it applies with full force here. Everything described above is visible to everyone. Reading the chain correctly is not an edge over professionals. It is protection against the specific error of buying a story that the bond market priced out three months ago.

Before your next discretionary equity decision, write down three things: what government bond yields have done over the last three months, what has happened to credit spreads, and whether the shares you are considering derive their value mainly from near or distant profits. If the first two have moved against the third, your thesis needs a reason why — and if you cannot supply one, you have learned something for the cost of ten minutes.
A worked reading makes the chain concrete, and shows what it does and does not tell you.

Government bond yields have risen sharply over three months. Credit spreads have widened. You are considering a company valued almost entirely on profits expected after 2035. The chain says the two moves you have already observed work directly against the third position, through both the discount rate and the economic channel. That does not mean the company is a bad business or that the shares must fall. It means your thesis now owes an explanation for why this company is an exception, and if you do not have one, you have been reading the last link and calling it news.

Do not convert this into market timing. The evidence that anyone reliably switches between regimes in advance is weak, and Chapter 4 Lesson 1 showed what the attempt costs the people who make it most often. Regime mapping tells you which pillar to trust in the environment you are already in. It does not tell you what the environment will be next quarter.
One further asymmetry is worth naming because it recurs in every case study in Chapter 5.

Regimes change gradually on the way up and abruptly on the way down. A trending market can persist for years and give many opportunities to notice it. A shift into stress can complete within days, and correlations converge before most participants have accepted that the environment changed. Any plan that depends on reacting to a regime change is depending on the slower of the two, and it is the faster one that causes the damage.

blocks.text: What to look for as a standing habit rather than an occasional exercise. Watch government bond yields and credit spreads even if you hold neither, because they move first. Note whether market leadership is broad or concentrated in a few names, which distinguishes a healthy trend from a narrow one. Notice when volatility has been unusually low for an unusually long time, since that is the condition in which leveraged positions accumulate. And be honest when the answer is that nothing aligns, which is more often than a market commentary industry can afford to admit.
One element of the chain matters more to readers outside the largest markets than to anyone inside them.

If you hold global equities but spend in a different currency, your return has two parts: what the shares did, and what the currency did. A year in which global markets rose 8% and your home currency strengthened 8% is a flat year for you. The shares performed exactly as reported, and none of it reached you.

This is not an argument for avoiding foreign holdings, which would return you to the home bias Chapter 2 Lesson 5 warned about. It is an argument for knowing that the currency is a live part of the position, for checking whether any fund you hold is currency-hedged, and for expecting a gap between the return quoted in the fund's reporting currency and the return you actually experienced.

quiz.question: Why do companies whose value rests on distant future profits move most when interest rates change?
options: Because they carry more debt than other companies
Because a higher discount rate reduces the present value of distant cash flows most, and rates also slow the economy those profits depend on
Because they are usually smaller and therefore more volatile
Because index funds are forced to sell them when rates rise
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Rates hit equities through two channels at once. A higher discount rate reduces the present value of all future cash flows and reduces distant ones most, and higher rates also slow the economy generating those cash flows. A high multiple is a bet on distant profits, which is precisely the bet a rate rise damages.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Debt levels, size and index mechanics all exist, but the main effect is arithmetic: a higher discount rate reduces the present value of distant cash flows far more than near ones, and a high multiple is by definition a claim about distant profits.

quiz.question: Why does regime mapping not amount to market timing?
options: Because regimes are always obvious in advance
Because it tells you which pillar to trust in the environment you are already in, rather than predicting the next environment
Because it applies only to bonds and currencies
Because timing the market is prohibited for retail investors
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The evidence that anyone reliably anticipates regime changes is weak, and Chapter 4 Lesson 1 showed the cost of trying. The value of reading the regime is defensive: it stops you applying a momentum thesis in a market that has stopped trending, or buying a story the bond market priced out months ago.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Regimes are ambiguous while you are inside them and clear only in hindsight — that is precisely why this is not timing. What the exercise offers is knowing which kind of evidence has power in current conditions.

quiz.question: Why is a plan that depends on reacting to a regime change unreliable?
options: Because regime changes are never observable
Because regimes shift gradually upward but abruptly downward, and it is the abrupt shift that causes the damage
Because reacting to markets is always irrational
Because regime changes only affect leveraged positions
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A trending market gives you years to notice it. A shift into stress can complete within days, with correlations converging before most participants accept the environment has changed. A reactive plan is calibrated to the slower transition and meets the faster one.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Regime changes are observable after the fact, and they affect unleveraged holdings too. The problem is the asymmetry in speed: the damaging transition is the fast one, and a plan built on reacting will be too late for it.

keyTerms.def: The prevailing environment of risk appetite, volatility and trend.
The path a policy change takes across markets, reaching equities late.
A market where no pillar aligns and the correct discretionary position is none.

lessons.title: Portfolio Discipline and the Long Game
lessons.keyIdea: Diversification weakens exactly when it is needed, because correlations rise in falling markets and not in rising ones. Discipline is what you built in advance to survive that.

blocks.text: This is the last lesson in the track. It is about what happens to a portfolio as a whole, over years, rather than to any position inside it.

Chapter 2 Lesson 5 gave the case for diversification and the honest answer on how many holdings is enough. There is one property of diversification that lesson deferred, and it is the most important thing to know about it.

Longin and Solnik, in Extreme Correlation of International Equity Markets, published in the Journal of Finance in 2001, tested whether international equity market correlation rises in volatile periods. Using extreme value theory to model the tails of the joint distribution, they found the increase in the negative tail — falling markets — but not in the positive tail. Correlation between markets rises when they fall together, and does not rise when they rise together.
The tendency of separate markets to move together far more closely during sharp falls than during normal or rising periods.

This is diversification's central limitation and it must be stated plainly. The protection is weakest exactly when you need it. A portfolio spread across countries behaves like several different investments for years, and then, on the worst days, behaves like one. Anyone who tells you geographic diversification protects you in a crisis is describing the average day rather than the day that matters.

Note what this is not. It is not an argument against diversifying — the alternative is being concentrated on the worst days as well as the ordinary ones. It is an argument against expecting diversification to deliver in the drawdown what it delivers in the sample average.

That is also why the fat tails thread from Foundations Chapter 3 and Forex Chapter 5 returns here. Extreme joint moves are more frequent than a model assuming a normal distribution predicts, and Longin and Solnik's method exists precisely because that assumption fails in the tail. They reject multivariate normality for the negative tail and not for the positive one.
Against a portfolio that occasionally behaves as one thing, the defence is not a better forecast. It is the set of rules you wrote before it happened.
Rebalancing, from Chapter 4 Lesson 3, is the first of them, and it deserves an honest framing rather than a promotional one.

Rebalancing is not a forecast. It does not claim the asset you are buying will now outperform. It is a rule that holds your risk where you decided it should be, and its main effect is on the risk you carry rather than on the return you earn. Whether it adds return depends on the period, and anyone quoting a rebalancing bonus as a reliable figure is extrapolating from a sample.

A portfolio set at 60% equities and left alone through a long bull market can arrive at 80% equities without a single decision having been made. The investor did not choose more risk. They simply did not act, and the market chose for them. Rebalancing is what makes that a decision again.
The second discipline is reviewing decisions separately from outcomes.
Examining a closed decision for whether the reasoning and the rules were sound, rather than only for whether it made money.

Forex Chapter 6 Lesson 4 made this point and it transfers without modification. A good decision can lose money and a bad one can make it. If you only review the losers, you learn nothing from the positions that worked for reasons you never identified — and you will repeat them at a larger size.

Once a year, read your plan from Chapter 4 Lesson 3 alongside what you actually did. Note every place they differ. For each difference, write whether the plan was wrong or the deviation was. Both happen. Only one of them is a reason to change the document.
A closing word on what this track has and has not given you.

It has given you what a share is, what an index and an ETF actually do, what you pay to own them, how to read a company, what the evidence says about factors and efficiency, how risk and sizing work in equities, what the behaviour and fee arithmetic really costs, three case studies where the popular account is wrong or incomplete, and a written process. That is a complete foundation, and it is deliberately not a set of recommendations.

It has not given you a way to know which shares will rise. Nothing can. Chapter 2 Lesson 4 explained why the search for that is harder than it looks, and Chapter 4 Lesson 1 showed what the search costs the people who attempt it most actively.

Running the six-pillar process properly on individual companies is genuinely time-consuming, and many people who understand it completely will still decide they would rather not do it themselves. Scere Training sells completed trade theses built with this framework for readers in that position. That is the only mention it gets, and the reason the framework is taught in full here is that you should be able to judge such a thesis — including one of ours — rather than take it on trust.

The discipline described in this chapter is unglamorous and it is where the results are. A written plan, a rebalancing band, a known total fee, an uninterrupted contribution schedule, and the habit of checking a confident claim against its source. None of it requires predicting anything, and every one of the three case studies in Chapter 5 would have been survived by someone doing only these things.
It helps to see what correlation clustering does to a portfolio in numbers rather than as a principle.

An investor holds five regional equity funds. In ordinary years they move somewhat independently, and the portfolio is visibly steadier than any one of them. In a severe global downturn all five fall together, and the portfolio falls about as far as the worst of them. The diversification did not fail — it delivered exactly what the historical average said it would, and the average was assembled mostly from ordinary years.

The correct response is not to abandon diversification but to stop relying on it alone. Holdings that are genuinely different in kind, rather than in region, and cash held outside the market, are what remain effective when equity correlations converge. Chapter 3 Lesson 1 made this point from the risk side; it is the same conclusion reached from the portfolio side.

Be sceptical of any product marketed on its diversification benefits using a correlation figure measured over a full sample. The number you need is the correlation during the worst 5% of months, and it is almost never the number in the advertisement. Longin and Solnik's contribution was precisely to measure the tail rather than the average.

blocks.text: What to look for once a year, as the closing habit of this track. Recalculate what each holding is as a percentage of the whole, since drift has been working all year. Recalculate your total recurring fees, since providers change them. Confirm your contribution schedule ran without interruption. Reread your written plan and note where reality diverged from it. And check that the reason you hold each position is still the reason you originally wrote down, rather than a new reason invented to justify keeping it.

quiz.question: What did Longin and Solnik find about correlation between international equity markets?
options: Correlation is constant across all market conditions
Correlation rises in the negative tail — when markets fall together — but not in the positive tail
Correlation rises in both rising and falling markets equally
Correlation falls during volatile periods, improving diversification
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Using extreme value theory to model the tails, they rejected multivariate normality for the negative tail but not the positive one. That is diversification's central limitation: the protection is weakest exactly when it is needed, because separate markets behave like one thing on the worst days and like separate things on ordinary ones.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The finding is asymmetric. Correlation rises when markets fall together and does not rise when they rise together — which means diversification delivers least in precisely the conditions people hold it for.

quiz.question: An investor holds five regional equity funds. In a severe global downturn all five fall together and the portfolio falls about as far as the worst of them. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The diversification failed and was never real
It delivered what the historical average promised, but that average was assembled mostly from ordinary years — correlations converge in the tail
The funds were secretly holding identical companies
Regional diversification is always useless
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Longin and Solnik found correlation rises in the negative tail and not the positive one. The protection was real in ordinary years and weakest in the worst ones, which is the honest description of what diversification buys — and the reason to hold things that are different in kind, plus cash, rather than relying on region alone.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. The funds held genuinely different companies and the diversification was real for most of the period. What the episode shows is the asymmetry: separate markets behave as one thing during sharp falls, so the average correlation overstates the protection available when it matters.

quiz.question: How should rebalancing be described honestly?
options: As a reliable source of extra return, since selling high and buying low adds value
As a rule that holds risk where you decided it should be, whose effect on return depends on the period
As a forecast that the underperforming asset will now recover
As an optional activity with no measurable effect
quiz.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Rebalancing makes no claim about what happens next. Its reliable effect is on the risk you carry: a 60% equity allocation left alone through a long rise becomes 80% without any decision being made. Whether it adds return depends on the period, and a quoted rebalancing bonus is an extrapolation from a sample.
quiz.feedbackWrong: Not quite. Rebalancing has a clear and measurable effect on risk, but it is not a forecast about the asset being bought and its return benefit is period-dependent rather than reliable. Its real job is keeping your allocation where you chose to put it.

keyTerms.def: Separate markets moving together far more closely during sharp falls than during normal periods.
Judging a closed decision by the quality of its reasoning rather than only by its result.
